observation_summary: The StringUtils.equals(CharSequence, CharSequence) method was using object equality (cs1.equals(cs2)) for CharSequence types, which is undefined behavior according to the JavaDoc for CharSequence. This caused failures when comparing different implementations of CharSequence that represent the same character sequence.
hypothesis: The StringUtils.equals(CharSequence, CharSequence) method incorrectly relies on the .equals() implementation of the CharSequence objects, which is not guaranteed to be consistent across different implementations (e.g., StringBuilder vs String). The fix requires comparing the character sequences character-by-character instead of relying on the object's .equals() method.
prediction: The implementation of StringUtils.equals(CharSequence, CharSequence) will show a direct call to cs1.equals(cs2) without checking if the sequences are equivalent in content when they are not the same type.
experiment_rationale: The bug report explicitly states that the implementation relied on CharSequence#equals(Object) which is undefined. The fix involves changing the comparison logic to be character-by-character, which is a procedural/algorithmic change to the method's logic.
reasoning_summary: The defect is a failure to correctly implement the equality check for the CharSequence interface. The code was using the default object equality, which is not valid for CharSequence. The fix is to implement a character-by-character comparison, which is a change to the method's algorithm.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While the fix involves adding a check (instanceof String), the core issue is the incorrect algorithmic approach to comparing CharSequences, which requires a character-by-character comparison rather than just a guard.
